issues.failure_explanation: The proof derives the needed pointwise identities q(u,u)=u and q^{(0,1)}(u,u)=1/2 only by matching Taylor coefficients for the functions lambda f^*, i.e. only for u=lambda f^*(a) with lambda in (lambda_-,lambda_+). For an integrand whose value at a lies outside this interval the hypotheses impose no constraint on q at (f(a),f(a)), and the conclusion can fail: take q equal to the logarithmic mean near the orbit of f^*(x)=e^x (scalably exact on it, f^*(a),f^{*'}(a) nonzero) but smoothly extended with q(-5,-5)=0; then for f=-5 (constant, in C^2) the error is |0-(-5h)|=5h, not o(h^2). The universal quantification over C^2(a,a+h) is stronger than what is proved and is false as stated.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the conclusion to functions f with f(a) in {lambda f^*(a): lambda in (lambda_-,lambda_+)} (a neighbourhood of f^*(a)).
issues.overall_effect: The lemma's error guarantee is established only for integrands whose value at a lies in the scaling interval of f^*(a); the advertised 'no worse than the trapezoidal rule on general functions' holds only in that local sense. No downstream labelled result is invalidated, since later uses need only the pointwise relations at the orbit points.
issues.title: Lemma lem:noworse concludes o(h^2) error for all C^2 functions, but the proof only covers values in the scaling orbit of f^*(a)
issues.why_classification: The repair is a one-clause local restriction; the error rate, the method, and every later use of the lemma are unchanged; only the never-used universal quantifier is narrowed.

issues.failure_explanation: The symbol f in the statement is never introduced. The proof computes q^{(0,2)} at the single point \bar f^*=(f^*(a),f^*(a)) and substitutes it into an expansion about the diagonal, so it establishes the formula only for f=f^*. At other points of the scaling family the coefficient changes: applying the same argument to lambda f^* gives q^{(0,2)} at ((lambda f^*(a),lambda f^*(a))) equal to -(1/(6 lambda)) f^{*''}(a)/[f^{*'}(a)]^2, so for f=lambda f^* the correct coefficient is -(1/(12 lambda)) f^{*''}(a)/[f^{*'}(a)]^2, not the printed one; for a general integrand the coefficient is not determined by the hypotheses at all. Only the reading f=f^* makes the displayed formula true.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the expansion for f=f^* (equivalently, at the base point (f^*(a),f^*(a))), or include the factor f^*(a)/f(a) for anchor values lambda f^*(a) in the scaling family.
issues.overall_effect: The corollary as written is ambiguous and false under its natural general reading. The following 'improved trapezoidal rule' paragraph defines a new q by the formula, so no labelled result inherits the error.

issues.failure_explanation: Two omitted hypotheses. (i) q_1 (and hence q_2, \hat I_1, \hat I_2) involves f^{*-1} and is defined only when the integrand's values lie in R; e.g. for f^*=e^x, R=(0,infty) and the rule is undefined for integrands taking non-positive values, so an error guarantee 'for f in C^4(R)' is ill-defined/unsupported without a range hypothesis on f. (ii) The error-order proof invokes Corollary cor:pders, whose nondegeneracy hypotheses f^*(a)!=0, f^{*'}(a)!=0 are not assumed in the theorem; at a critical point of f^* the inverse and hence q_1 need not be smooth (for f^*=x^3, q_1(f_0,f_1)=(1/4)(f_0^{1/3}+f_1^{1/3})(f_0^{2/3}+f_1^{2/3}) is not C^1 at (0,0)), so the Taylor-expansion step does not apply there.

issues.failure_explanation: Each trapezoidal piece T_k = xi_k(f(a)+f(a+xi_k h))/2 + (1-xi_k)(f(a+xi_k h)+f(a+h))/2 reproduces the first two Taylor terms with coefficient 1 (T_k[1]=1, T_k[x]=a+h/2), so \hat I = h sum_k alpha_k T_k matches I[f] at orders h and h^2 only if sum_k alpha_k = 1. This constraint is neither imposed nor verified: the displayed (n-1)x(n-1) system only enforces the j=2..n moments, so the proof establishes at most exactness on degrees 2..n and never uses that n is odd. The missing constraint is essential: for even n the same (uniquely solvable) system yields a rule that is not Newton-Cotes - e.g. n=2 gives alpha_0=2/3, i.e. \hat I = (h/3)(f(a)+f(a+h)), which is not even exact on constants, instead of the trapezoidal rule (h/2)(f(a)+f(a+h)). For odd n the conclusion is nonetheless correct: by node and weight symmetry (xi_{n-1-k}=1-xi_k, w_k=w_{n-1-k}) the n-point Newton-Cotes rule is representable as sum_k alpha_k T_k, hence by unique solvability coincides with the constructed rule, and then sum_k alpha_k = 1 holds - but this argument is entirely absent.

failure_location.quote: and hence demanding that the Taylor expansion of $\hat{I}[f]$ matches that of $I[f]$ up to order $h^{n+1}$ amounts to the $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ linear equation system

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the representability argument: show that for odd n the Newton-Cotes weights on nodes xi_k can be written in the trapezoid-combination form sum_k alpha_k T_k (using the symmetry of nodes and weights), which by uniqueness identifies the solution and yields sum_k alpha_k = 1; equivalently, append the constraint sum_k alpha_k = 1 to the system and prove its consistency for odd n.
issues.overall_effect: The corollary's proof does not establish its statement; the statement itself is true for odd n (confirmed by the representability argument and by the n=3,5 examples in the paper). No other labelled result depends on it.
issues.title: Proof of cor:added-4 never imposes exactness on constants (sum of alpha_k = 1), so the identification with the Newton-Cotes rule is not established, and the odd-n hypothesis is never used
issues.why_classification: The result survives intact, but the repair requires a contained nontrivial argument (existence of the trapezoid-combination representation of the Newton-Cotes rule, which is exactly where the parity of n enters); this is more than a routine local fix, yet needs no new global proof architecture and loses no content.

issues.failure_explanation: The matrix entries are evaluations p_j(xi_k) of the polynomials p_j(xi)=xi^j-xi+1, j=2..n, at the n-1 nodes xi_0..xi_{n-2}. Linear independence of the p_j as polynomials (different degrees) does not by itself imply that their evaluation matrix on finitely many points is invertible; evaluation can destroy independence. The claimed fact is true - if P=sum c_j p_j vanishes at all nodes, then P(0)=sum c_j forces sum c_j=0, so P=xi^2 Q with deg Q <= n-2 vanishing at xi_1..xi_{n-2}, i.e. Q=c prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(xi-xi_k), and 0=P(1)=c prod(1-xi_k) with prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(1-xi_k)=(n-2)!/(n-1)^{n-2} != 0 forces c=0 - but this (or an equivalent Vandermonde-type) argument is not given; the stated reason is invalid as an inference.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper's own corollary states that the construction yields the n-point Newton-Cotes rule. For n=3,5 these are indeed Simpson's and Boole's rules, but the 7-point closed Newton-Cotes rule (weights proportional to (41,216,27,272,27,216,41), exact through degree 7) is not Weddle's rule (3h/10)(f_0+5f_1+f_2+6f_3+f_4+5f_5+f_6): Weddle's rule already fails to integrate x^6 exactly (on [0,6] with unit spacing it gives (3/10)*133320 = 39996, while the integral is 6^7/7 = 279936/7 approx 39990.86), so it cannot equal the degree-7-exact Newton-Cotes rule. The sentence misidentifies the n=7 output of the construction.

failure_location.quote: One easily verifies that Simpson's ($n=3$), Boole's ($n=5$) and Weddle's ($n=7$) rules are recovered in this way.

issues.overall_effect: A factual mislabeling in a closing remark of the section; the formal content of cor:added-4 and the rest of the paper are unaffected.
issues.title: Passing claim that the construction recovers Weddle's rule is incorrect: it yields the 7-point Newton-Cotes rule, which differs from Weddle's rule

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims the displayed formula has o(h^4) error. Writing g=log f and L=g(a+xi h)-g(a+(1-xi)h), the printed rule expands as q = f(a) e^M (1 + L/2 + L^2/12 - L^4/180 + ...); at the Gauss nodes xi=(3-sqrt3)/6 the order-h^3 term of \hat I = h q is f(a)(G_2/6 + G_1^2/9) h^3 (G_k = g^{(k)}(a)), whereas the exact integral requires f''(a)/6 h^3 = f(a)(G_2+G_1^2)/6 h^3. Hence |\hat I[f]-I[f]| = f'(a)^2/(18 f(a)) h^3 + O(h^4) for positive smooth f; e.g. for f=e^x on [0,h], \hat I = h + h^2/2 + h^3/9 + O(h^4) versus I = h + h^2/2 + h^3/6 + O(h^4). So as printed the formula is only O(h^3) (second order), not o(h^4). With the opposite sign, q = (f_0-f_1)/log(f_0/f_1) + (1/12)(f_0-f_1) log(f_0/f_1), the L^2 coefficient becomes 1/4 and all coefficients through order h^4 match (G_2, G_1^2 at order h^2 give 1/6, 1/6; G_3, G_1 G_2, G_1^3 at order h^3 give 1/24, 1/8, 1/24), so the claimed o(h^4) property is correct with the flipped sign.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Flip the sign of the correction term to + (1/12)(f_0-f_1) log(f_0/f_1) (equivalently, reverse the logarithm's argument in that factor).
issues.overall_effect: An isolated illustrative claim in the outlook is false as printed (the formula is second-order, not o(h^4)); the subsequent remark connecting the nodes to 2-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature presupposes the claimed accuracy. Nothing else in the paper depends on it.
issues.title: The displayed 'o(h^4)' two-point formula in the outlook is only second-order accurate as printed (sign error in the correction term)
issues.why_classification: A single-sign correction fully restores the claimed o(h^4) property (verified by the expansion); the remark is isolated with no dependents, so no substantive claim elsewhere is affected.
